0.title: Afraid, and Going Anyway
0.essay:
You know what you ought to do. Report the figures honestly. Tell your friend the hard truth. Go to the hospital appointment. Take the step that God’s word plainly asks of you. And your heart is pounding, your mouth is dry, and every part of you wants to find another way. If you know that feeling, this study is for you.

Courage for ordinary Christians

We tend to think of courage as something for soldiers and martyrs. But ordinary Christian life asks for it every week: courage to do the right thing when it will cost you, to keep going when you cannot see the outcome, to speak the truth kindly, to suffer without giving up, and in the end to face illness and death.

The Bible does not treat courage as a gift for a few. It commands it, again and again, to frightened people. And every time, the command rests on a promise: “for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:9). That is the heart of this study. Christian courage is not confidence in ourselves. It is doing what is right while we are afraid, because God is with us.

Where we are going

We will look at what courage is and is not, where it comes from, and above all at Jesus, who set his face to go to the cross for cowards like us. Then we turn to courage when the right thing is costly, courage in uncertainty, suffering and death, and practical help for the moment and afterwards, including after failure.

The studies The Fear of Man (disapproval and standing), Contentment & Anxiety (worry), Knowing God’s Will (decisions) and Handling Conflict (speaking up) sit close by; this study builds on them rather than repeating them.

The chapters

What Courage Is, and Is Not; For the LORD Your God Is with You; He Set His Face; The Right Thing at a Cost; Into the Unknown and Through the Valley; and In the Moment and Afterwards.

For reflection

Where in your life right now do you need courage? What is the thing you know you should do, but are afraid to?

1.title: What Courage Is, and Is Not
1.essay:
Many Christians quietly believe they are not brave people. They are cautious by nature, easily frightened, slow to speak. They assume courage belongs to someone else. Scripture tells a different story. Courage is not a personality type. It is a kind of faithfulness, and it is offered to the timid as much as to the bold.

Not the absence of fear

The first thing to say is the most freeing. Courage is not the same as feeling unafraid. If it were, God would never need to say “Be strong and courageous” to anyone. He says it because the people he is speaking to are frightened. Moses says it to Joshua in front of all Israel, and then the LORD says it to Joshua three times in one chapter (Joshua 1:6, 7, 9). Joshua was stepping into Moses’ shoes, with a river in flood ahead of him and walled cities beyond it.

David put it simply: “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you” (Psalm 56:3). Notice the word “when”, not “if”. The believer will be afraid. The question is what we do next. Courage is not the absence of fear. It is doing what is right while we are afraid, because we trust the God who is with us.

Gideon is a gentle example. God told him to pull down his father’s altar to Baal. He obeyed, but “because he was too afraid of his family and the men of the town to do it by day, he did it by night” (Judges 6:27). It is hardly heroic. Yet Scripture records that he obeyed. Shaking, at night, with ten servants: it still counted. God was patient with Gideon, and he is patient with us.

Not recklessness

Courage is also not recklessness. Running into danger for no reason, ignoring sensible advice, or taking risks to feel alive is not a virtue. “The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it” (Proverbs 22:3). Jesus told his disciples to be “wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10:16). Paul escaped from Damascus in a basket and more than once left a town when his life was threatened. That was not cowardice but stewardship of his life for God’s work.

So Christian courage does not mean staying in danger that God has not called you to bear. If you are being harmed or threatened at home, courage means getting to safety and telling someone who can help, including the police. It never means putting up with abuse in order to look strong or spiritual. Courage is not a call to be careless with your health or your safety either. It is a call to obey God, and God never commands foolishness.

Not temperament, and not bravado

Some people are naturally bold. They enjoy a confrontation and are not troubled by risk. That can be a gift, but it is not the same as courage. A bold person can be bold for the wrong things, or bold in a way that tramples others. And a quiet, shy person can show great courage, precisely because it costs them so much.

The clearest contrast in Scripture is between bravado and faith. On the night Jesus was arrested, Peter said, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you!” (Matthew 26:35). He meant it. But his confidence rested on his own loyalty and strength. Within hours he had denied his Lord three times. Bravado says, “I am strong enough.” Faith says, “I am not strong enough, but God is with me.” Bravado collapses when the pressure comes, because it was leaning on the wrong thing. Faith can tremble and still stand, because it is leaning on God.

The young David is the other side of the picture. Facing Goliath, he did not boast in his sling. “You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts” (1 Samuel 17:45). And again, “For the battle is the LORD’s” (1 Samuel 17:47). His courage looked outward to God. That is the mark of biblical courage. It is not loud self-belief. It is quiet God-belief.

Courage serves love

Finally, courage is never an end in itself. Paul writes, “Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love” (1 Corinthians 16:13–14). Courage is strength put at the service of what is good: obeying God and loving people. Christian courage is brave not to win or be admired, but to be faithful.

An example

A woman in her sixties has always thought of herself as a coward. She hates arguments and avoids hospitals. When her neighbour, a widower she barely knows, is taken ill, she feels she should visit him. For two days she finds reasons not to. On the third she prays in the car park, “Lord, I am frightened, but you are with me,” and goes in. She stays twenty minutes and reads him a psalm. Her hands shake the whole time. Nobody else would call it brave. God sees it as exactly that.

For reflection

Have you assumed that courage is for other kinds of people? How does it help to know that courage is not the absence of fear? Where have you seen the difference between bravado and faith in your own life? What small act of faithful courage might God be asking of you this week?

2.title: For the LORD Your God Is with You
2.essay:
If courage is not self-confidence, where does it come from? The Bible’s answer is consistent from Moses to Paul. It comes from God: from his presence with us, from his promises to us, and from his rule over everything that happens to us.

The promise inside the command

When Moses was about to die, he gathered Israel and said, “Be strong and courageous. Do not fear or be in dread of them, for it is the LORD your God who goes with you. He will not leave you or forsake you” (Deuteronomy 31:6). Then the LORD said the same to Joshua: “Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:9).

Notice the little word “for”. God never simply says, be brave. He says, be brave because I am with you. The command rests on a promise. Courage is not something we squeeze out of ourselves. It is the fruit of believing that God is really there, really for us, and really in charge. Through Isaiah God speaks to his frightened people in the same way: “fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand” (Isaiah 41:10).

The same promise is repeated to Christians: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). Jesus’ last words in Matthew’s Gospel are, “And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). Every Christian who has to face something hard does not face it alone.

Esther: “If I perish, I perish”

Esther was queen of Persia, but going to the king uninvited could cost her life. Her people faced destruction. Mordecai urged her, “And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14). Esther did not pretend to be unafraid. She asked her people to fast for three days, and then said, “Then I will go to the king, though it is against the law, and if I perish, I perish” (Esther 4:16).

The name of God does not appear in the book of Esther, yet his hand is everywhere in it. Her courage rested on a quiet trust that God was ruling over the king’s palace. She did not know how it would end. She knew what was right, and she left the outcome with God.

Daniel’s friends: “But if not”

Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refused to bow to the king’s golden image. Facing the furnace, they said, “our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods” (Daniel 3:17–18).

Those two words, “But if not”, are some of the bravest in Scripture. Their courage did not depend on being rescued. They believed God could save them. They hoped he would. But they would obey him either way. That is courage rooted in God himself rather than in a particular outcome. And they were not alone in the fire: the king saw a fourth figure walking with them.

Nehemiah and the apostles

When Nehemiah was rebuilding Jerusalem’s walls under threat of attack, he told the frightened workers, “Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers” (Nehemiah 4:14). The cure for fear was to remember God. Later, when he was urged to hide in the temple to save his life, he refused: “Should such a man as I run away?” (Nehemiah 6:11).

Peter and John were arrested for preaching about Jesus, and ordered to stop. The council noticed something. “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus” (Acts 4:13). Their answer was simple: “for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard” (Acts 4:20).

Paul too knew fear. In Corinth the Lord spoke to him at night: “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you” (Acts 18:9–10). Even the great apostle needed to be told not to be afraid, and the reason given was the same as Joshua’s: I am with you.

Sovereignty steadies the heart

Underneath all these stories is the truth that God rules. Nothing can happen to his people outside his wise and loving will. Jesus said of the sparrows, “not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father” (Matthew 10:29). This does not mean that his people never suffer. It means that suffering never has the last word, and never escapes his purpose. Jonathan, facing a Philistine garrison with only his armour-bearer, put it well: “nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few” (1 Samuel 14:6).

What a God this is! He is great enough to rule kings and furnaces, and near enough to walk into the fire with three young men. Courage grows when that God fills our view.

An example

A student is the only Christian on her course. When a group project involves something she believes is dishonest, she needs to say she will not take part. The night before, she reads Joshua 1:9 and writes on her hand the words “with you wherever you go”. Her voice wobbles, but she says it kindly and clearly. Afterwards two of the group quietly agree with her.

For reflection

Why do you think God’s commands to be courageous always come with the promise of his presence? Which of these examples, Esther, the three friends, Nehemiah, the apostles or Paul, speaks most to your situation? What would it mean for you to say “But if not”? Which promise of God’s presence will you hold on to this week?

3.title: He Set His Face
3.essay:
The bravest life ever lived was not that of a soldier or an explorer. It was the life of a carpenter from Nazareth who walked, step by step and with his eyes open, towards the cross. His courage is our pattern. Far more than that, it is our salvation.

He set his face

Luke marks a turning point in Jesus’ ministry: “When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51). Jesus knew what waited for him there. He had told his disciples plainly that he would be rejected, handed over and killed. He went anyway. The phrase echoes the Servant of the Lord in Isaiah: “But the Lord GOD helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set my face like a flint” (Isaiah 50:7).

The Servant’s resolve comes not from hardness but from trust: “the Lord GOD helps me.” Jesus went because he trusted his Father and loved his people.

Gethsemane: fear and obedience together

If we want to see what courage looks like from the inside, we must go into the garden. Mark tells us that Jesus “began to be greatly distressed and troubled. And he said to them, ‘My soul is very sorrowful, even to death’” (Mark 14:33–34). Luke adds that “being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground” (Luke 22:44).

This was no calm, untroubled hero. The Son of God, truly human, shrank from the cup of his Father’s wrath against sin. And he said so: “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36).

Here is the deepest picture of courage there is. Fear and obedience together. Jesus did not pretend he was not in anguish. He brought his anguish to his Father, honestly, and then surrendered his will. If you have ever told God you do not want something, and then asked for his will to be done, you have stood, in a small way, in Gethsemane. It is not a lack of faith to be afraid. Our Lord was “greatly distressed” too. And “we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15).

When the soldiers came, Jesus did not hide among the olive trees. “Then Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward and said to them, ‘Whom do you seek?’” (John 18:4). He stepped forward to be taken, so that his disciples could go free.

His courage was for us

That last detail matters. Jesus was not only showing us how to be brave. He was being brave in our place. That same night, “they all left him and fled” (Mark 14:50). Every disciple failed. Peter, who had promised to die with him, denied him three times and “broke down and wept” (Mark 14:72).

We are those disciples. We have kept quiet when we should have spoken, and run when we should have stood. The good news is that Jesus did not go to the cross for the brave. He went for the cowardly, the failing and the ashamed. He endured the cross, “despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2), and bore the punishment for all our sins, our cowardice included. Through his death he set free “all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:15).

Peter restored

The story of Peter does not end in the courtyard. Before it happened, Jesus had told him, “but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). After the resurrection the angel’s message was, “But go, tell his disciples and Peter” (Mark 16:7). Peter was singled out for welcome, not blame.

Then, beside a charcoal fire on a beach, Jesus asked him three times, “Do you love me?” Three denials were met by three questions and three commissions: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). Jesus did not discard the man who had failed; he gave him work to do.

A few weeks later the same Peter stood up in front of thousands in Jerusalem, the city where he had denied Jesus, and “lifted up his voice” (Acts 2:14). Not his temperament had changed, but his heart: he had met the risen Lord, been forgiven, and received the Holy Spirit.

The Spirit of power

The disciples were hiding behind locked doors “for fear of the Jews” when the risen Jesus came and stood among them, said “Peace be with you”, and breathed on them, saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:19–22). Courage is a gift of the Spirit, not a product of willpower. Paul wrote to timid Timothy, “for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control” (2 Timothy 1:7).

When the early church was threatened, they did not pray only for safety. They asked God to “grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness” (Acts 4:29), and “they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness” (Acts 4:31). The same Spirit lives in every believer today. He takes frightened people and, little by little, makes them brave like Jesus.

An example

A man in his forties once walked away from a friend who was being mocked for his faith, and laughed along. Years later he still feels sick about it. Reading John 21, he realises that Jesus did not ask Peter to explain himself, only whether he loved him. He confesses his failure to God, and then writes to the friend to apologise. The friend replies warmly. The man finds that he is less afraid of speaking about Christ than he was before he failed.

For reflection

What does Gethsemane teach you about being afraid and obedient at the same time? How does it change things to know that Jesus’ courage was for you, and that your failures of courage are forgiven? What does Peter’s restoration say to you about past failures? Will you pray, as the early church did, for boldness rather than only for safety?

4.title: The Right Thing at a Cost
4.essay:
Most of the courage the Christian life asks for is not dramatic. It is the courage to tell the truth in a meeting, to refuse to cut a corner, to stand beside someone who is being treated unfairly, or simply to say no. It rarely makes the news. But it may cost a promotion, a friendship or a quiet life.

Ordinary faithfulness under pressure

In Egypt, Pharaoh ordered the Hebrew midwives to kill the baby boys. “But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live” (Exodus 1:17). They were ordinary women doing their jobs, who saw that some orders could not be obeyed, and God dealt well with them.

Daniel, a senior official in Babylon, knew that a new law made prayer to anyone but the king a capital offence. “He got down on his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he had done previously” (Daniel 6:10). His courage was simply to keep doing what he had always done. He did not hide, and he did not make a show of it. Years earlier, as a young man, he had shown the same quiet resolve over the king’s food, and notice how he did it: he “asked the chief of the eunuchs to allow him” (Daniel 1:8). Courage and courtesy went together.

When the apostles were told to stop preaching, Peter answered, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). That is the line every Christian may one day have to draw. We owe real respect to employers, governments and those in authority. But when they require what God forbids, or forbid what God requires, we must obey God.

What it looks like now

For most of us, the pressure is quieter. A manager asks you to mislead a customer. Friends joke cruelly about someone who is not there, and expect you to join in. A colleague is being bullied, and nobody says anything. A friend is drifting into something that will hurt them, and you are the one who could speak. Someone wants a yes from you that you know should be a no.

Scripture calls us to speak for those who cannot speak for themselves: “Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute” (Proverbs 31:8). It calls us to honesty when lies would be easier, and to “speaking the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15). Sometimes the bravest word is a single, quiet sentence.

Count the cost

Jesus did not hide the price of following him. “For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost” (Luke 14:28), he asked. Courage is not naive. It looks honestly at what may be lost. You may be passed over. You may be laughed at. You may, occasionally, lose a job. It is wise to pray it through beforehand with a trusted Christian friend.

But having counted the cost, we also count the promises. “But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you will be blessed. Have no fear of them, nor be troubled” (1 Peter 3:14). And we hand the consequences to God: “let those who suffer according to God’s will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good” (1 Peter 4:19). Our job is to do what is right. The outcome is his.

Courage is not stubbornness

Here we need care. Not every stand is a brave one. Some people mistake stubbornness for conviction, or enjoy a fight and call it faithfulness. Some pick battles that are not theirs: “Whoever meddles in a quarrel not his own is like one who takes a passing dog by the ears” (Proverbs 26:17).

So it is worth asking honest questions. Is this a matter of right and wrong, or only of my preference? Is it my responsibility to speak, or someone else’s? Am I hoping to serve this person, or to win? “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all” (Romans 12:18).

Biblical courage is also gentle. Peter, who knew both cowardice and boldness, wrote: “in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15). And Paul: “the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone” (2 Timothy 2:24). Because they are secure in God, the bravest people rarely need to shout. The study Handling Conflict offers more on speaking up wisely.

A word about safety

Standing with the weak sometimes means raising concerns about abuse, at work, in a family or even in a church. That is right and brave. Do it through the proper channels: safeguarding officers, managers, and where needed the police or social services. If you yourself are being abused or threatened, courage does not mean staying and enduring it. It means getting to safety and telling someone who can help. God does not ask you to remain in danger to prove your faith.

An example

An accountant at a small firm is asked by the owner to move some costs into the next year so that the figures look better for a bank. He knows it is wrong. He lies awake counting the cost: he has a mortgage and two children. He prays, talks to his wife and an older friend from church, and then tells the owner respectfully that he cannot do it, and suggests an honest alternative. The owner is annoyed for a week, but the figures go in as they are. He does not know what will happen at his next review, but he sleeps again.

For reflection

Where are you under pressure to say or do something you know is wrong? What would it cost you to do the right thing, and what has God promised you if you do? How can you tell the difference, in your own heart, between courage and stubbornness? Is there someone weaker than you who needs you to speak up for them?

5.title: Into the Unknown and Through the Valley
5.essay:
Some situations need courage not for one brave moment but for a long road whose end we cannot see. A move, a new job, a child born with special needs, a diagnosis, a long illness, death drawing near. Here courage looks less like charging forward and more like taking the next step, and the next, holding on to God’s hand.

Not knowing where he was going

God said to Abram, “Go from your country and your kindred and your father’s house to the land that I will show you” (Genesis 12:1). Not a land already shown, but one he “will show”. Hebrews comments: “By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8).

Abraham had a promise, not a map. He knew who was calling him, but not where the road would lead. That is often our situation too. We would like to know how the treatment will go, whether the move will work out, what the next ten years will hold. God rarely tells us. He gives us himself, his promises, and enough light for the next step. “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105).

So courage in uncertainty is mostly a matter of one step of obedience at a time. Jesus said, “Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble” (Matthew 6:34). We are asked to be faithful today, and to trust God with the rest. “He who observes the wind will not sow” (Ecclesiastes 11:4): if we wait for perfect certainty, we will never act. The study Knowing God’s Will gives more help with the decisions themselves; here the point is the courage to walk on once the path is clear enough.

Faith that walks without seeing

Abraham’s family “all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar” (Hebrews 11:13). They did not see how it all ended. Yet they kept going, because “they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God” (Hebrews 11:16). God is not ashamed of people who walk in the dark holding on to his word.

When King Jehoshaphat faced an army he could not resist, he prayed, “We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you” (2 Chronicles 20:12). That brave prayer turns helplessness into trust.

Courage in suffering and illness

Illness tests courage in its own way. It is often long, and it wears us down. Courage here is rarely heroic. It looks like going to the next appointment, taking the treatment, telling the truth to the doctor, letting others help, praying when you can manage only a few words, and refusing to give up on God.

Paul knew bodily weakness well. “So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). He did not deny the wasting away, but he saw something unseen and eternal happening too. At one point he says he and his companions “despaired of life itself”, and adds, “But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead” (2 Corinthians 1:8–9).

Courage in illness is never a reason to refuse sensible medical care or to ignore your doctor in the name of faith. Using medicine is part of trusting God, not a lack of it.

Courage at the end

Death is the last enemy, and Christians are not asked to pretend otherwise. But we are given reasons to face it bravely. “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me” (Psalm 23:4). The valley is real. So is the Shepherd.

Paul, in prison and not knowing whether he would live or die, wrote that his hope was “that with full courage now as always Christ will be honored in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:20–21). Near the end of his life, deserted by friends, he wrote, “But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me” (2 Timothy 4:17), and, “The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom” (2 Timothy 4:18).

This courage rests on what Christ has done. He went into death and came out the other side. He has taken the sting from it: “The sting of death is sin … But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:56–57). To Martha at her brother’s grave he said, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live” (John 11:25). The believer does not walk into the dark alone, and does not walk into the dark for ever. Beyond it is a face, and a home.

The study Death, Dying & Heaven and the study Christian Suffering say more about these things.

An example

A man in his fifties is told that he has a serious cancer, and that treatment may or may not work. The first weeks are terrifying. A friend suggests that he stop trying to see the whole road and pray each morning only for that day. He begins each day with Psalm 23 and one small aim: get to the clinic, ring his sister, read to his grandson. Some days he weeps. But he keeps putting one foot in front of the other, and his family notice a steadiness in him they had not seen before.

For reflection

Where are you being asked to go forward without knowing how things will turn out? What is the next single step of faithfulness in front of you? How do Paul’s words in Philippians 1:20–21 help you think about illness or death? Which promise from this chapter would you want to hold on to in the valley?

6.title: In the Moment and Afterwards
6.essay:
Courage is learned slowly, in small things, with God’s help. Here is some practical wisdom for before the hard moment, during it, and afterwards, whether it went well or badly. None of it is a technique for feeling brave. It is a way of leaning on the God who is with you.

Before: pray, prepare and count

If you can see the hard moment coming, bring it to God early. Tell him plainly what you are afraid of. “I sought the LORD, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears” (Psalm 34:4). Pray, as the early church did, not only for safety but for boldness and for the right words.

Think it through. What exactly is the right thing to do? What might it cost? What is the kindest and clearest way to say it? It may help to write down the sentence you need to say. Preparation is not a lack of faith: Nehemiah prayed, and also set a guard (Nehemiah 4:9).

Do not go alone

God often gives courage through other people. When David was hunted and afraid, “Jonathan, Saul’s son, rose and went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hand in God” (1 Samuel 23:16). “Two are better than one … For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10). Tell a trusted Christian friend what you are facing. Ask them to pray, and perhaps to check in with you afterwards. For a serious wrong, such as fraud or abuse, seek experienced advice and use the proper channels.

In the moment: a short prayer and a true word

When the moment comes, your body will probably react: a racing heart, a tight chest, a dry mouth. That does not mean you lack faith. Breathe slowly. Pray a few words, as Nehemiah did before the king (Nehemiah 2:4): Lord, you are with me; help me.

Then remember one promise. You will not be able to recall a whole chapter, so choose one or two in advance and keep them close:

“fear not, for I am with you” (Isaiah 41:10).
“for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:9).
“When I am afraid, I put my trust in you” (Psalm 56:3).
“for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control” (2 Timothy 1:7).
“Yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36).

Jesus promised his disciples that when they had to speak under pressure, “what you are to say will be given to you in that hour” (Matthew 10:19). The Spirit of the Father is with us when our preparation runs out.

Small faithful steps

You do not have to do everything at once. Do the next right thing. Make the one phone call. Say the one sentence. Go to the one appointment. “One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much” (Luke 16:10). Every small act of trust makes the next a little easier, not because you have become strong, but because you have found God faithful.

Afterwards, when it went well

Give thanks to God. The strength was his: “we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us” (2 Corinthians 4:7). And leave the consequences with him. Doing the right thing does not always bring a good result straight away. You may still face cost. Keep entrusting yourself to him “while doing good” (1 Peter 4:19).

Afterwards, when you failed

Sometimes you will fail: stay silent, say yes when you meant no, or run. When that happens, do not hide from God. Go to him. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). Remember Peter, wept over and then welcomed. Jesus’ courage on the cross covers your cowardice too.

Then get up again. “For the righteous falls seven times and rises again” (Proverbs 24:16). If you can still put something right, do it. If you cannot, leave it with God and be ready for next time. And be kind to your body. When Elijah fled in fear and asked to die, God did not scold him. He let him sleep, and sent an angel to say, “Arise and eat” (1 Kings 19:5). “For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14).

When fear becomes something more

For some people, fear has become an anxiety disorder: panic attacks, constant dread, avoiding ordinary life, or fear that will not settle however much they pray. This is common and very treatable. Please see a doctor or a qualified counsellor as well as praying and reading Scripture. Medicine, where it is prescribed, is a good gift of God, not a failure of faith. The study Contentment & Anxiety says more.

If fear or despair ever leads to thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, please get help now. Call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), and tell someone you trust. Your life is precious to God.

An example

A young dad has avoided telling his non-Christian brother that he has become a Christian. He keeps meaning to, and keeps failing. He tells a friend at church, who prays with him. He picks one verse, 2 Timothy 1:7, and one sentence to say. At a family barbecue his heart is thumping, but he says it simply. His brother shrugs and changes the subject. It is not the conversation he imagined, but it is out in the open, and a month later his brother asks him about it.

Going on

Courage is a life of small steps taken with God. “Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the LORD!” (Psalm 31:24). The one who set his face to go to Jerusalem has gone ahead of you, and walks beside you now. “And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

For reflection

What hard moment can you see coming, and how could you prepare for it with God and with a friend? Which verse from this study will you carry with you? What is the next small, faithful step in front of you? If you have failed recently, what would it look like to go to Jesus and then get up again?
